questionsCatalog.title: A1. Shortest Path in an Unweighted Network
questionsCatalog.description: A college network contains N computers connected by network links. Every link has the same cost. Given a source computer and a destination computer, find the minimum number of links required to reach the destination.
questionsCatalog.explanation: Because all edges have equal cost, BFS explores the graph level by level and guarantees the shortest path in terms of number of edges.

questionsCatalog.title: A2. Explore All Reachable Nodes
questionsCatalog.description: Given a network starting from computer S, visit every reachable computer by exploring as deeply as possible before returning to previous nodes.
questionsCatalog.explanation: The required exploration strategy is depth-first traversal.

questionsCatalog.title: A3. Cheapest Route Between Cities
questionsCatalog.description: There are N cities connected by roads. Every road has a positive travel cost. Find the minimum-cost route from city S to city T.
questionsCatalog.explanation: All edge weights are positive and only a single-source shortest path is required.

questionsCatalog.title: A4. Shortest Path with Negative Edge Costs
questionsCatalog.description: A transportation network contains roads whose costs may be positive or negative. Find the shortest distance from a source to every other vertex and determine whether a negative-weight cycle exists.
questionsCatalog.explanation: Bellman-Ford supports negative edge weights and can detect negative-weight cycles.

questionsCatalog.title: A5. Shortest Distance Between Every Pair
questionsCatalog.description: A small transportation network contains N cities. Find the shortest distance between every pair of cities.
questionsCatalog.explanation: The requirement is all-pairs shortest paths, which is the primary application of Floyd-Warshall.

questionsCatalog.title: A6. Minimum-Cost Cable Network
questionsCatalog.description: A university wants to connect all its buildings using network cables. Each possible cable has a different cost. Connect all buildings with minimum total cable cost. The input is provided as a list of weighted edges.
questionsCatalog.explanation: The problem is a Minimum Spanning Tree problem, and the edge-list representation makes Kruskal particularly suitable.

questionsCatalog.title: A7. Minimum Network from a Starting Building
questionsCatalog.description: A university wants to connect all buildings with minimum total cable cost. The network is represented using an adjacency matrix, and construction starts from a specified building.
questionsCatalog.explanation: Prim's grows the Minimum Spanning Tree from a starting vertex and works naturally with an adjacency matrix.

questionsCatalog.title: A8. Search from Both Ends
questionsCatalog.description: A large unweighted network has a known source and destination. Find the shortest route by searching simultaneously from both the source and destination until the searches meet.
questionsCatalog.explanation: The problem specifically benefits from simultaneous search from both endpoints.

questionsCatalog.title: A9. GPS Navigation
questionsCatalog.description: A GPS system needs to find a shortest route between two locations. The system knows the actual cost traveled so far and also has a valid estimate of the remaining distance to the destination.
questionsCatalog.explanation: A* combines the cost already travelled with a heuristic estimate of the remaining cost.

questionsCatalog.title: A10. Heuristic-Based Robot Navigation
questionsCatalog.description: A robot is moving toward a target. At every step, it examines neighboring positions and chooses the position that appears closest to the target according to a heuristic. The objective is to reach the target quickly rather than guarantee the globally shortest route.
questionsCatalog.explanation: The algorithm repeatedly chooses the locally most promising neighboring state.

questionsCatalog.title: B1. Search an Unsorted List
questionsCatalog.description: You are given an unsorted list of student IDs. Determine whether a particular ID exists in the list. Only one search operation is required.
questionsCatalog.explanation: The data is unsorted and only one search is required. Sorting first would add unnecessary work.

questionsCatalog.title: B2. Search a Sorted List
questionsCatalog.description: A college stores student IDs in ascending order. Given an ID, determine whether it exists. The list contains up to 1,000,000 IDs.
questionsCatalog.explanation: The list is already sorted, allowing the search space to be halved at every step.

questionsCatalog.title: B3. Sort a Small Dataset
questionsCatalog.description: Sort a small collection of numbers in ascending order. Constraints: N <= 50, O(1) additional memory is preferred, simple implementation is preferred.
questionsCatalog.explanation: For a very small dataset with constant auxiliary space and simple implementation, Selection Sort is the intended choice.

questionsCatalog.title: B4. Sort a Nearly Sorted Array
questionsCatalog.description: A list of student marks is already almost sorted. Only a small number of elements are out of position. Sort the complete list.
questionsCatalog.explanation: Insertion Sort performs very well when the number of inversions is small.

questionsCatalog.title: B5. Guaranteed Worst-Case Sorting
questionsCatalog.description: A large dataset must be sorted. The system requires a guaranteed worst-case time complexity of O(N log N).
questionsCatalog.explanation: Merge Sort guarantees O(N log N) worst-case complexity, while standard Quick Sort can degrade to O(N²).

questionsCatalog.title: B6. Fast In-Place Sorting
questionsCatalog.description: A large array needs to be sorted efficiently. The application prefers an in-place algorithm and is primarily concerned with average-case performance.
questionsCatalog.explanation: Quick Sort is generally efficient in practice, has good average-case performance, and can be implemented in-place.

questionsCatalog.title: B7. Search One Million Sorted IDs
questionsCatalog.description: A database contains one million student IDs in sorted order. The system receives many search queries and must determine whether each ID exists.
questionsCatalog.explanation: The data is already sorted, so Binary Search provides O(log N) search per query.

questionsCatalog.title: B8. Find a Pair with a Given Sum
questionsCatalog.description: Given a sorted array of N <= 100,000 integers and a target value T, determine whether two different elements have a sum equal to T. Constraints: Array is already sorted, O(1) extra space.
questionsCatalog.explanation: Two pointers can solve the problem in O(N) time and O(1) extra space.

questionsCatalog.title: B9. Maximum Sum Without Adjacent Elements
questionsCatalog.description: You are given an array where each element represents the value of a house. You cannot select two adjacent houses. Find the maximum total value that can be collected. Example: Input [2, 7, 9, 3, 1] -> Output: 12 (Selection: 2 + 9 + 1 = 12).
questionsCatalog.explanation: The problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure. The solution can be built from solutions to smaller prefixes.

questionsCatalog.title: B10. Find a Pair in a Sorted Array
questionsCatalog.description: Given a sorted array of N <= 200,000 integers and a target value T, determine whether two numbers add up to T. Constraints: Array is already sorted, O(1) additional space, target complexity: O(N).
questionsCatalog.explanation: Place one pointer at each end. Move the left or right pointer depending on whether the current sum is smaller or larger than the target.
